title: Linear Regression
tagline: The straight line through your data. Simple, interpretable, and the foundation of almost everything else.
what_it_is: Linear regression is a way to predict a number (like house price) from one or more input numbers (like square footage, bedrooms, age). It assumes the relationship is a straight line. You find the line that minimizes the sum of squared errors between the predicted values and the actual values. With one input, it is a simple line: y = slope * x + intercept. With multiple inputs, it is a plane or hyperplane: y = w1*x1 + w2*x2 + ... + b.
key_points: Predicts a continuous number, not a category.
Assumes a linear relationship between inputs and output.
The coefficients (weights) tell you the expected change in output for a one-unit change in that input, holding others constant.
The intercept is the predicted value when all inputs are zero.
Minimizes the sum of squared residuals (differences between actual and predicted).
why_it_exists: Before machine learning was a thing, people needed a simple way to model relationships. Linear regression was invented in the 1800s. It exists because many relationships are approximately linear, and even when they are not, linear regression gives a simple baseline. It is fast, easy to explain, and the coefficients give direct insights: 'each additional bedroom adds $30,000 to the house price'. More complex models might be more accurate but harder to understand. Linear regression is the starting point.
what_it_measures: The coefficients measure the effect of each input. A coefficient of zero means that input has no linear relationship with the output. The R-squared value measures how much of the variance in the output is explained by the inputs. The p-values (in statistics) tell you if a coefficient is significantly different from zero. The residuals (errors) tell you if the straight line assumption is reasonable.
intuition: Imagine you sell lemonade. You notice that on hotter days, you sell more cups. You plot temperature on the x-axis and cups sold on the y-axis. You draw a straight line through the cloud of points. That line is linear regression. For any new temperature, you follow the line up to see predicted cups. The line might say: for every 10 degrees hotter, you sell 5 more cups. That is the slope. When temperature is zero (not realistic), you would sell 2 cups – that is the intercept. Simple.

breakdown.means: predicted value of y (e.g., house price)
intercept – value when x is zero
slope – change in y for a one-unit change in x
total squared error the line tries to minimize

when_to_use: When you need to predict a continuous number (sales, temperature, price).
When you want an interpretable model – the coefficients tell a story.
When the relationship between inputs and output is roughly linear, or you are okay with a linear approximation.
As a baseline model. Always try linear regression first before complicated methods.
When you have a small dataset. Linear regression works well with few examples.
when_not_to_use: When the relationship is clearly non-linear (e.g., U-shaped or periodic). A straight line will be terrible.
When there is severe multicollinearity (two inputs are almost the same). Coefficients become unstable. Use ridge regression instead.
When you have more features than samples (p > n). Ordinary linear regression fails. Use regularization (lasso or ridge).
When your output is a category (yes/no). Use logistic regression instead.
common_mistakes: Interpreting a coefficient as causal. 'One more bedroom adds $30k' – only if all other things are equal, which they never are in real data.
Forgetting to scale features. Coefficients of different magnitudes are not comparable without scaling.
Using linear regression on non-linear data and then being surprised by poor predictions.
Ignoring outliers. One extreme point can completely change the line because squared errors blow up.
ds_usage: In Python, you use `from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression`. Fit with `model.fit(X_train, y_train)`. Coefficients are `model.coef_`, intercept is `model.intercept_`. Predict with `model.predict(X_test)`. Evaluate with MAE, MSE, RMSE, or R². For statistical inference (p-values, confidence intervals), use `statsmodels` instead of scikit-learn.
